strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: privacy-preserving use of stored/shared video foundation model features, which is practically distinct from pixel-level anonymization.
The latent adapter formulation is simple, modular, and computationally attractive; freezing large video encoders and anonymizing feature embeddings is a plausible and useful design point.

Evaluation is broader than most prior video privacy work, covering action recognition, temporal action detection, anomaly detection, multiple encoders, several training datasets, and useful ablations on losses, adapter architecture, task training, and scale.

Empirical results show a strong privacy-utility tradeoff on the reported VISPR attribute prediction protocol, with small drops in downstream utility relative to raw features and substantially better utility than prior pixel anonymization baselines.
The paper makes a good effort to connect privacy preservation with bias mitigation and includes additional protocols/results on perceived-gender subgroup gaps.
weaknesses: The privacy evaluation is not strong enough to fully support the central privacy claims. Most results rely on a limited private-attribute classifier protocol, and the paper does not evaluate adaptive or stronger attackers, nonlinear probes with varied capacity, white-box attackers aware of the anonymizer, reconstruction/inversion attacks, membership-style risks, or attacks trained directly on anonymized features under realistic threat models.

There is no formal privacy guarantee. The mutual-information language is intuitive but not rigorously established; maximizing an NT-Xent-style loss between static clips does not by itself prove removal of sensitive information, especially when latent consistency explicitly preserves much of the original representation.

The method does not reliably protect temporal private attributes: the gait experiment shows that latent consistency preserves substantial gait recognition signal. This is an important limitation for video privacy, since many sensitive attributes are temporal or behavioral.

Baselines are incomplete for the proposed latent-feature setting. The paper mostly compares to pixel-level anonymization methods, but lacks strong latent baselines such as adversarial attribute removal, gradient reversal, noise/projection/compression methods, representation disentanglement, or privacy-utility optimization with learned probes.

The fairness/bias contribution is less convincing than the privacy contribution. The NTU bias protocol is artificially constructed, the gender formulation is binary and based on perceived gender, and annotation/ethics details are thin; subgroup-gap reductions are promising but not enough to establish robust bias mitigation.

Some claims are overstated, especially around generalizable anonymization and removal of private information. The results demonstrate reduced probe performance under particular protocols, not broad anonymization against determined attackers.

Reproducibility is only moderate: many implementation details are present, but the paper would benefit from clearer splits, attacker-training details, code/model release commitments, variance over runs, and significance estimates for the main tables.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: privacy leakage from stored video foundation model features, which is a realistic deployment concern not fully addressed by pixel-level anonymization methods.
The latent adapter formulation is practically appealing: it is lightweight, plug-and-play with frozen video encoders, and potentially avoids expensive retraining or re-extraction pipelines.

The evaluation spans multiple downstream video tasks, including action recognition, temporal action detection, and anomaly detection, which is broader than much prior work in video privacy preservation.

The paper includes useful ablations on training losses, task combinations, adapter architecture, latent consistency weight, and training data scale, which helps clarify the role of several components.
weaknesses: The privacy evaluation is not strong enough to support the central claims. Privacy is mostly measured by downstream attribute classifier accuracy/cMAP, apparently with relatively weak or fixed attackers. There is no evaluation against adaptive attackers, stronger probing models, inversion/reconstruction attacks, membership/linkability risks, or attackers aware of the anonymizer.

The method provides no formal privacy guarantee. Claims such as reducing mutual information or preserving privacy are much stronger than what the contrastive proxy objective and classifier-based evaluations establish.

The proposed privacy objective is conceptually under-justified. Maximizing an NT-Xent loss between static clips is presented as mutual information minimization, but the paper does not rigorously show that this removes sensitive information rather than merely degrading the chosen probe features.

The evaluation exposes a key limitation: temporal private attributes such as gait remain substantially recognizable when latent consistency is used. This is serious for video privacy, yet it is treated mostly as a limitation rather than addressed by the method.

Baseline comparisons are not fully convincing. Prior pixel-level methods are mostly compared under I3D, while the paper’s main motivation concerns modern VFMs; there are few comparisons to feature-space sanitization, adversarial representation learning, information bottleneck, noise-based, or differentially private baselines.

Several reported results weaken the headline claims. For larger models, temporal action detection drops can be sizable, e.g. VideoMAEv2-G THUMOS14 falls from 70.09 to 62.69/65.21, which is not within the advertised 1-2% utility loss.

The bias mitigation contribution is underdeveloped. The NTU protocol uses an artificial binary perceived-gender shortcut with a single action example, and the Toyota Smarthome analysis reports only coarse subgroup accuracy gaps. This is insufficient evidence for broad claims about mitigating gender bias.

The work relies on binary perceived-gender labels and sensitive attribute prediction protocols, but the ethical framing and annotation validity are limited. The paper acknowledges the binary limitation but does not deeply address risks of reinforcing problematic demographic categories.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. The project page appears blank in the PDF, implementation details are partial, and it is unclear whether code, splits, gender annotations, pretrained adapters, and probing protocols will be released.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially statements that the method is the first generalizable approach, that it strongly reduces privacy leakage, and that it promotes equitable video understanding. The evidence supports a useful empirical tradeoff, not these broader conclusions.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: privacy preservation for reusable video foundation model features, rather than only pixel-level anonymization for a single task.
The latent anonymization formulation is practically appealing: the adapter is lightweight, plug-and-play with frozen encoders, and avoids retraining large video backbones.
The empirical evaluation is broad for this area, covering privacy leakage, action recognition, temporal action detection, anomaly detection, multiple backbones, and larger video foundation models.
Results show a strong privacy-utility tradeoff: substantial reductions in VISPR private-attribute predictability with only small drops on most utility tasks.
The ablations are useful and support the roles of the privacy loss, utility loss, latent consistency loss, task co-training, AAM architecture, and training dataset scale.
The paper includes an interesting additional angle on gender-presentation bias evaluation, and shows that the proposed anonymization can reduce subgroup performance gaps.
weaknesses: The privacy evaluation is not fully convincing against realistic adaptive attackers. Most evidence relies on classifier performance on anonymized features, but stronger nonlinear probes, white-box/adaptive attackers, feature inversion, reconstruction attacks, or attacks trained with knowledge of the anonymizer are not sufficiently explored.

The method provides empirical obfuscation rather than formal privacy guarantees. Claims such as privacy preservation should be qualified because sensitive information may still be recoverable by stronger attacks or by attributes not covered in VISPR/Casia-B.

The comparison to prior pixel-level anonymization methods is somewhat imperfect, since those methods were designed for narrower settings and may not be optimized for the same foundation-model, multi-task feature-sharing scenario.

The temporal sensitive attribute result is mixed: with latent consistency, gait recognition remains fairly high, suggesting that the method may preserve some private temporal signatures exactly when they overlap with utility-relevant information.

The proposed gender bias protocols are promising but limited: they use binary perceived gender labels, partly synthetic imbalance, modest absolute improvements, and no clear statistical significance analysis.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, especially around general privacy preservation and bias mitigation. The evaluation supports reduced leakage for selected attributes and tasks, but not broad protection of arbitrary private information.
Reproducibility details are decent, but the paper would be stronger with released code, trained adapters, exact splits for the bias protocols, and more information about variance across runs.

strengths: Timely and meaningful problem: preserving privacy for stored/shared video foundation model features is well motivated, and the latent-space framing is a practical alternative to pixel-level anonymization.
The proposed anonymizing adapter is lightweight and plug-and-play with frozen encoders, which is attractive for large VFMs where retraining or re-extracting transformed videos is costly.

Empirical scope is broad: results cover action recognition, temporal action detection, anomaly detection, retrieval, several backbones including larger models, and multiple privacy datasets/protocols.
Ablations are useful and generally support the roles of the privacy objective, utility objectives, latent consistency, architecture choice, task co-training, and training data scale.
The paper discusses bias mitigation and proposes concrete perceived-gender bias protocols, which adds an interesting secondary angle beyond attribute leakage reduction.
weaknesses: The privacy threat model is not fully convincing. The method substantially reduces attribute prediction but does not eliminate leakage, and the white-box inversion setting largely recovers private attribute prediction, which is a serious concern for deployments where the adapter or training recipe may be known.

Privacy evaluation relies heavily on classifier performance/cMAP rather than stronger adaptive attacks, calibrated leakage measures, or formal guarantees. The high random-chance cMAP values in some tables make the practical meaning of the reported leakage reductions harder to interpret.

Some central claims are stronger than the evidence, especially claims about removing spatial information or general privacy preservation. Temporal sensitive attributes such as gait are only weakly protected when latent consistency is used, which undercuts the claim of broad privacy preservation.

The comparison to prior work is imperfect: several baselines are pixel-level methods tied to older architectures, while the paper would benefit from stronger feature-space/adversarial baselines, supervised privacy baselines across all settings, and modern privacy-preserving action-recognition methods where applicable.

The method appears targeted to global clip embeddings, limiting applicability to dense or generative video tasks. This is acknowledged, but it narrows the claimed generality for video foundation models.

The bias evaluation is promising but preliminary: binary perceived-gender labels, limited datasets/actions, unclear annotation reliability, and modest absolute changes make it insufficient to strongly support broad fairness claims.

Reproducibility details are moderate but incomplete for a top-tier privacy/vision paper: code/resource availability is unclear, and several protocols such as inversion attacks, gender annotation, and feature extraction settings need more precise specification.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: privacy preservation for stored/shared video foundation model features, which is practically distinct from pixel-space anonymization.
The proposed latent adapter is computationally attractive: it keeps the encoder frozen, can use precomputed features, and is evaluated across several video tasks rather than only action recognition.

The empirical section is broader than many privacy-anonymization papers, including action recognition, temporal action detection, anomaly detection, retrieval, multiple backbones, ablations over losses/architectures/tasks, and some inversion-attack analysis.
The paper is generally readable and the high-level formulation is easy to follow.
weaknesses: The central privacy claims are not convincingly supported. Reducing attribute cMAP by a relative percentage is not the same as achieving privacy; several reported post-anonymization scores remain high, and random/chance baselines are missing for key privacy evaluations such as VISPR. The paper therefore overclaims privacy preservation.

The threat model is weak and too favorable. The method explicitly fails under the white-box inversion setting, yet white-box or semi-white-box access is plausible when releasing a model-side anonymizer or deploying a standardized feature pipeline. This substantially weakens the claimed privacy guarantee.

The evaluation lacks strong adaptive privacy attackers. Most privacy results appear to rely on standard classifier probes; there is little evidence against stronger attackers with different architectures, larger training sets, contrastive objectives, side information, membership/linkability attacks, or attackers aware of the anonymization objective.

Baselines are incomplete and partly unfair. Comparisons focus heavily on pixel-level prior work, often using I3D, while the proposed method is a latent adapter for modern frozen encoders. Missing baselines include simple feature noise, bottleneck/projection, adversarial gradient-reversal probes, supervised private-attribute removal, information bottleneck methods, and task-agnostic representation release methods.

The methodological novelty is moderate. A trainable adapter with utility retention, latent consistency, and adversarial/self-supervised privacy loss is a reasonable combination, but the components are conceptually standard and the paper does not establish a strong theoretical or empirical reason that maximizing the NT-Xent loss reliably removes sensitive information rather than merely weakening a limited probe.

The gender-bias contribution is underdeveloped. The NTU protocol is artificially constructed, the Toyota Smarthome analysis is small, binary perceived gender is ethically and methodologically fraught, and there is no clear annotation protocol, uncertainty analysis, or statistical significance testing. The bias mitigation claims are stronger than the evidence.

The privacy-utility tradeoff is not fully characterized. Some results show nontrivial drops on TAD or anomaly detection depending on training data, and temporal sensitive attributes such as gait are explicitly not protected when latent consistency is used, which conflicts with the broad framing of privacy preservation for video understanding.

Reproducibility is limited. The manuscript gives many implementation details, but the project page appears blank in the extracted manuscript, and important details such as exact splits, attacker training protocols, hyperparameter selection, and confidence intervals/statistical variance are insufficient for assessing robustness.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: privacy-preserving use of stored/shared video foundation model features is important, and the latent anonymization framing is a meaningful shift from prior pixel-level anonymization work.
The proposed AAM is practical: it is lightweight, plug-and-play with frozen video encoders, supports precomputed features, and is evaluated on multiple backbones including larger VFMs.

Evaluation is broad and convincing overall, covering privacy leakage, action recognition, temporal action detection, anomaly detection, retrieval, multiple datasets, several backbones, and comparisons to prior anonymization methods.

The paper includes useful ablations on loss components, task combinations, training data scale, AAM architecture, latent consistency weight, and attention heads, which support the main design choices.
The empirical privacy-utility tradeoff is strong in the main setting: large VISPR cMAP reductions with small utility drops across several downstream tasks.
The additional gender-bias protocols and results are an interesting secondary contribution, showing that latent anonymization can reduce subgroup gaps without an explicit fairness objective.
weaknesses: The privacy guarantee is empirical and threat-model dependent. There is no formal privacy guarantee, and the white-box inversion results substantially recover private attributes, which weakens claims of robust privacy preservation.

The method does not consistently suppress temporal sensitive attributes: gait recognition remains fairly high with latent consistency, and removing latent consistency harms generalization. This reveals an important privacy-utility limitation for motion-based identity cues.

The evaluation mainly targets global clip embeddings; the paper acknowledges that dense tasks such as segmentation or captioning are out of scope, limiting the generality of the claimed foundation-model anonymization.

Some comparisons to prior methods are imperfect because older pixel-level baselines are mostly evaluated with I3D, while the strongest results use newer latent backbones. This is understandable but makes the relative advantage partly confounded by representation choice.

The bias evaluation is promising but still limited: perceived gender is binary, subgroup labels/protocol construction may be sensitive, and the reported fairness improvements are based on small gap changes without uncertainty estimates or broader demographic evaluation.

The private-attribute reductions on VP-HMDB51/VP-UCF101 are more modest than the headline VISPR numbers, suggesting that privacy protection against video-level private attributes is not uniformly strong.
